This video is misleading because AMD software (or any other software such as hwinfo which reads the same sensors) only reports power draw from the GPU and not the whole card. AMD improved their DX11 performance in their May 2022 driver (22.5.2) but it won't boost the performance on every title out there. Radeons simply don't report full power consumption of the card. Your mistake is to assume they do like green team cards. Techpowerup used PCAT to measure true power consumption from slot and pcie power cables(probably techtesters did too). I have RX 6800, it's 250W TGP card. However wattage in monitoring is max ~200W, also stock PPT is 203W(from hwinfo). I know it consumes 250W rather than 200W based on wall figures. I think radeons leave out VRM losses, gap is about same as losses would be.
You card is boosting normally, in techpowerup review average clock speed was 2500MHz. Your card is hitting same numbers, it's clearly not receiving less power. For me there's nothing wrong with your card. If you want to have confirmation, ask techtesters to report power consumption figure from monitoring software. 
Performance differences can be caused by many things. For example, did you have ReBAR on? Techpowerup did. They also used AMD system which have a bit higher gain from ReBAR when using Radeon. Or did you test exact same scenes in the game? If not, numbers are not comparable because games do not run at flat.

I had a similar issue with my ASUS Strix 6800XT a few months ago. DDU did nothing and it was not a hardware issue. it might not be a Gigabyte issue as this is a problem that quite a number of users have encountered on various 6000 series cards (reference included). The card simply refused to draw the proper power draw (220W max) and the coil whine was god-awful. In fact, it drew 100W playing CSGO on 1440p max settings, with FPS  varying wildly between 60 - 400. 

What I found to work for my specific card is to disable SAM in adrenalin and then turning off "Enable above 4G decoding" in BIOS before running DDU. After that, I will install the new driver, re-"enable above 4G decoding" in BIOS before booting and turning on SAM in the adrenalin software. I'll re-input my overclocks and it will draw the correct 300 - 330W value for my card. I more or less repeat this step whenever a new driver acts up and it usually solves the problem. Perhaps this could be the solution for the Gigabyte 6950XT.

As an electronics designer I can assure you that the massive component shortage is not just about GPU's or CPU's. There's a shortage of every type of component. This forces vendors to look for alternative components, Their first choice are drop in replacements, meaning that the new component can be soldered to the same PCB providing identical performance. Once you can't get your hands on such drop in replacements you basically have three choices:
1. Redesign the PCB to achive the same performance with other components. 
2. Choose a replacement that can be fitted to the same PCB but with less performance, life span, reliability etc.
3. Stop producing. 
With massive coil whine, your performance issues and the lack of vendor explanations I would guess at number 2. The board is not able to supply enough power thus throttled by a hidden setting that you can't touch. Or possibly the board can supply enough power but was throttled by mistake. Should you recieve a magic wand special update bios I'd guess for the latter.

Dawid Does Tech Stuff : did you use 3 separate PCI-Ex cables to power the RX 6950 XT ? Usually if you have too weak of a PSU (not in terms of watts but in terms of amperage capability through each 12 V line), daisy chaining the PCI-Ex cables (those little parasitic additional 8-pin cables that modern PSU-s have two on each PCI-Ex cable) manifests itself in too little amperage that the GPU needs to perform at 100 % of power capacity.
But it also could be a a few partially damaged VRM modules due to previous owners not using a custom fan curve to cool the whole PCB down properly. If 2 of the power stages are damaged, the controller goes into a power safe mode AKA more of a conservative model to protect the GPU core.

​ @robertb6276  Yes, the 11900k was worse in gaming than the 10900k, and was also worse in many other tasks than the 10900k because it had two less cores and four less threads!  It was probably their worst release EVER, and that's saying something.
The 11400f and 11600 (non-k) are hidden gems in the 11th generation of Intel CPU's though.
I had a 9600k (no hyperthreading and PCIE Gen 3) on my PC, with a GTX 1070.  I sold the 9600k and Z390 motherboard for £200 and my GTX 1070 for £300 in eBay auction during the hardware drought in the lockdowns.
I found an i5-11600 for £100 (which reaches 4.8ghz with the power limits disabled), and is basically an 11600k since the 11600k can only overclock to 4.9ghz!  You will get maybe 2 FPS more on an 11600k than an 11600.  
Then I found a B560 ASUS Tuf Gaming motherboard for £80, and bought a Radeon RX 6600 xt on release week for £350 (it had been returned and the box was damaged as well as the Display Port lead being missing from the box.   It was an ASUS ROG Strix model, so one of the best.  
Because the 11600 has PCIE Gen 4, some games had their framerate massively increased on the 6600 xt.  Doom Eternal went from 165 FPS on my 9600k to over 220 FPS at 1080p Ultra Nightmare settings on the 11600.  A few other games showed massive improvements from the 9600k to the i5-11600, mostly it was a 5-10 FPS increase though. The new GPU was what made the difference!  I upgraded the CPU because I think in the next year or so, a 6 core and 6 thread CPU won't be able to play the latest games without stuttering.  Hyperthreading is going to matter more and more going into the future. 
I managed to sell my 9600k, Z390, and GTX 1070, buy an i5-11600, B560 board, and RX 6600 xt, and increase my framerate by (on average) 50% for £30 - under $50!
In general the 11th Gen from Intel sucks though.  The i3 and i5's were decent, but I have seen benchmarks where the i5-11600k had the same FPS as the 11900k in Cyberpunk 2077 and Red Dead 2, and BEAT the 11700k by a couple of FPS!!!
I wanted a 3060 ti and a Ryzen 5800x but that would have cost me maybe £700 to upgrade, and for only another 20% performance increase than my current upgrade. $50 for 50% more FPS was a HUGE bargain for me.

comments.text: Just going to add my MSI experience here. I've dealt with a lot of their cards, but I've never bought a new graphics card, always used.
